name: Ashikaga shogunate
info: The feudal military government of Japan during the Muromachi period, ruled by the Ashikaga clan from Kyoto, remembered for arts shaped by Zen Buddhism, Noh theatre and its slide into the Sengoku wars.

facts.successor: Sengoku period; rule of Oda Nobunaga

t: Ashikaga Takauji set up his military government in Kyoto in 1336 after overthrowing the Kenmu Restoration of Emperor Go-Daigo.
It was the weakest of Japan's three military governments, depending on the loyalty of the daimyō because the shōgun held little territory of his own.
Oda Nobunaga drove the fifteenth shōgun, Ashikaga Yoshiaki, out of Kyoto in 1573, ending the shogunate.
dyk: The name Muromachi comes from the Muromachi district of Kyoto, where the third shōgun, Ashikaga Yoshimitsu, built his residence known as the "Flower Palace" in 1379.
ev: Ashikaga Takauji establishes his own military government in Kyoto, overthrowing the Kenmu Restoration
Ashikaga Yoshimitsu establishes the "Flower Palace" on Muromachi Street in Kyoto
The Southern Court gives up and the Northern and Southern Courts are combined into one
The death of Ashikaga Yoshinori leaves the authority of the bakufu almost vanished
The Ōnin War breaks out among the daimyō, beginning the Sengoku period
The shōgun Ashikaga Yoshiteru is assassinated, and Oda Nobunaga installs Ashikaga Yoshiaki as his puppet
Oda Nobunaga drives Ashikaga Yoshiaki out of Kyoto, ending the shogunate

sections.foundation:
From 1180 to 1185 the Genpei War between the Taira and Minamoto clans ended with the victory of Minamoto no Yoritomo and the founding of the Kamakura shogunate, later dominated by the Hōjō clan. The Hōjō monopoly of power, and the lack of a reward of lands after the defeat of the Mongol invasions, left their vassals resentful. In 1333 Emperor Go-Daigo called on local vassals to oppose Hōjō rule in the Kenmu Restoration. Sent by Kamakura to crush the rising, Ashikaga Takauji turned against the shogunate for reasons that remain unclear and helped overthrow it.

Go-Daigo's policies were unpopular and failed to satisfy those who had fought for him. In 1336 Takauji set up his own military government in Kyoto and made himself shōgun. A dispute with Go-Daigo over how to govern led Takauji to have Prince Yutahito installed as Emperor Kōmyō, while Go-Daigo fled the capital. Japan was divided between a Northern Court in Kyoto under Ashikaga influence and a Southern Court in Yoshino, the beginning of the Nanboku-chō period.
sections.socioeconomy:
The shogunate gave more attention to the arts and to trade than to gaining control of surrounding territories. It traded with Joseon Korea, using the daimyō of Tsushima Island as middlemen, and with imperial China, where goods were exchanged and labelled as offerings from one emperor to another. Ashikaga Yoshimitsu expanded these relations, receiving large quantities of porcelain, silk and bronze coins from China and sending swords, lumber and ores in return. Marginal trade with Southeast Asia sent similar goods, together with furs, for spices and other kinds of lumber.

The economic base of the old order shifted to the provinces. The shugo appointed by the shogunate absorbed the judicial, economic and taxation powers of the local Imperial governors, and government holdings in each province passed rapidly into the personal holdings of the daimyō and their vassals. The Imperial court lost both its political weight and its economic base.
sections.military:
For 56 years the Northern and Southern Courts struggled for power. The Northern Court usually dominated, but the Southern Court was occasionally able to capture the capital; each time it was pushed back by the larger Northern armies. The struggle ended in 1392, under the third shōgun, when the Southern Court gave up and the two courts were combined.

Because Takauji had little personal territory, the military power of the shōgun depended on the loyalty of the daimyō, and the regime was weak militarily. Bloody succession crises among the warrior families wore down its authority, and the daimyō feuded among themselves for power. The Ōnin War of 1467 to 1477 turned these feuds into open warfare and began the constant civil war of the Sengoku period. In 1565 the shōgun Ashikaga Yoshiteru was assassinated, and the daimyō Oda Nobunaga used the opening to install Yoshiteru's brother Ashikaga Yoshiaki as shōgun.
sections.governance:
The Ashikaga shogunate is described as the weakest of the three Japanese military governments. Unlike the Kamakura shogunate before it or the Tokugawa shogunate after it, it relied heavily on the prestige and personal authority of the shōgun. The centralised master-vassal system of Kamakura gave way to a highly decentralised system of daimyō, local lords whose authority grew far beyond that of Kamakura times.

The Imperial court was no longer a credible threat. The failure of the Kenmu Restoration had left it weak and subservient, and Takauji reinforced this by placing his government near the Emperor in Kyoto. Powers lost by the court passed to the shōgun, and this position reached its peak under Ashikaga Yoshimitsu. After him the structural weakness of the regime was exposed by repeated succession crises and early deaths. The list of shōgun runs to fifteen, from Ashikaga Takauji to Ashikaga Yoshiaki, with gaps and a second reign for Ashikaga Yoshitane.
sections.impact:
The Ashikaga era was a period of great development in Japanese culture and art, with Zen Buddhism as a large contributor. The tea ceremony moved from a large open room to a small, quiet setting and became a form of meditation. Flower arranging became an art of spiritual value, its arrangements often used as offerings to the Buddha. Noh theatre was created in this period; its performances were enjoyed and protected by nobles and elites, and helped to widen the themes of shows and to produce poetry. The performing arts suffered during the Ōnin War but recovered once power had fully shifted.

Abroad, the shogunate's contacts with Joseon and with China shaped its foreign relations, and its trade carried Japanese swords, lumber and ores across the sea. The name of the Muromachi district of Kyoto, where Yoshimitsu built his residence, gave the period its name.
sections.decline:
The authority of the bakufu had almost vanished by 1441, at the death of Ashikaga Yoshinori. After the Ōnin War the shogunate was reduced to little more than a local political force in Kyoto. The puppet shōgun Ashikaga Yoshiaki, installed by Oda Nobunaga in 1568, was not wholly subservient: he struck bargains with the monasteries and mediated between powerful clans such as the Otomo and Mori. In 1573 Nobunaga drove him out of Kyoto, and the shogunate was destroyed. Yoshiaki fled first to Shikoku and later received the protection of the Mōri clan in western Japan.

The Ashikaga family survived the 16th century, and a branch of it became the daimyō family of the Kitsuregawa domain. The site of the "Flower Palace" in Kyoto, bounded by Karasuma, Imadegawa, Muromachi and Kamidachiuri streets, is marked by a stone, and relics and excavations of the area are kept in the Kanbai-kan of Dōshisha University.

summary: The Ashikaga shogunate ruled Japan from Kyoto between 1336 and 1573, after Ashikaga Takauji overthrew the Kenmu Restoration. Weak in land and arms, it leaned on the daimyō, reached its height under Ashikaga Yoshimitsu, fostered Zen arts and Noh, and dissolved into the Sengoku wars until Oda Nobunaga ended it.
